name: Nominative determinism
statement: People are said to drift towards careers, towns and spouses whose names resemble their own, because they like the letters in their own name.
meaning: Two different claims travel under one label. The weak one is a collector's joke: urologists called Splatt and Weedon exist, and they are funny. The strong one is causal and belongs to Brett Pelham and his co-authors, who named it implicit egotism. Most people hold favourable views of themselves, those views attach to the letters in their names, and the resulting preference is supposed to tip the largest decisions a person makes. Only the second claim is testable, because only it predicts a countable excess: more Dennises among dentists than the base rate for the name allows. The joke cannot be tested at all, since nobody records the dentists called Lawrence. The laboratory preference the argument is built on is covered under the name-letter effect, entry no. 134, and its numeric twin under the birthday-number effect, entry no. 171.

origin.who: Feedback, the New Scientist column, crediting the reader C. R. Cavonius
origin.note: Two columns did the work, and both were read for this entry on the New Scientist site. On 5 November 1994 Feedback paired a book on the polar regions by Daniel Snowman with a guide to subterranean London co-written by Richard Trench, then quoted Jen Hunt of the University of Manchester in The Psychologist: "Authors gravitate to the area of research which fits their surname." Her example was a paper in the British Journal of Urology by Splatt and Weedon, and readers were invited to send more. The name arrived six weeks later. The column of 17 December 1994 reports "evidence supporting the hypothesis (which C. R. Cavonius suggests should be called Nominative Determinism) continues to pour in from readers", and refers back to items of 5 November and 3 December. John Hoyland, who created Feedback, is widely named as the coiner; the column credits a reader. The psychological claim is eight years younger than the phrase and comes from Pelham, Mirenberg and Jones in 2002.

evidence: Pelham, Mirenberg and Jones ran ten archival studies in 2002, mostly on the Social Security Death Index and on professional directories. Deceased women named Mildred and Virginia were distributed across Milwaukee and Virginia Beach in the predicted direction, chi-square(1) = 38.25, and the men named Jack and Philip across Jacksonville and Philadelphia more strongly still, chi-square(1) = 202.05. Across 35 American city names beginning with Saint, 445 women lived in the city matching their first name against 308.8 expected, 44% above chance, chi-square(1) = 41.97; for men the figures were 3,956 against 3,476.0, or 14% above, chi-square(1) = 58.63. The career studies are the famous ones and the smallest. Comparing dentists with lawyers in eight states, the female result reached chi-square(1) = 4.72 and the male result did not reach significance at chi-square(1) = 2.14. A supplementary national count found 482 dentists named Dennis against 257 named Walter and 270 named Jerry, three names of near-identical census frequency, an odds ratio of 1.83. Among published geoscientists there were 93 called George or Geoffrey against 65.5 expected, chi-square(1) = 4.58.

replication.headline: Simonsohn reproduced the original patterns and then found confounds large enough to account for all of them, in marriage, occupation and moving alike.
replication.detail: Marcello Gallucci got there first. Reanalysing the published tables in 2003, he found 74 names or numbers that allow a reliable test, of which 55 gave no significant result, four gave a significant result against the hypothesis and 15 gave one in support. Those counts are read from his accepted manuscript in the Milano-Bicocca repository, the published version being closed. Uri Simonsohn's 2011 paper in the same journal ran 14 new studies against eight main findings of the Pelham group. He did not fail to replicate: his abstract says the article successfully replicates the original findings, and he calls the name-similarity effect in Pelham et al. robust and widespread. On dentists he used the same lawyer directory the original authors had used and counted 2,889 lawyers named Dennis against 1,411 named Jerry and 2,000 named Walter. That is a ratio of actual to expected frequency of 1.38 for Dennis-the-lawyer against 1.43 for Dennis-the-dentist, a difference of chi-square(1) = 1.28, p = .25. Dennis is a younger name than Walter, so more Dennises were still working. Georges and Geoffreys wrote 682 geoscience dissertations against 550.2 expected, ratio 1.24, and 25,351 dissertations in every other science against 19,250.6 expected, ratio 1.32, which makes them slightly less likely to pick geology than anything else. On states he took the whole Death Index, 80 million records, and the 5.97 million people born after the Social Security Act of 1935. People were disproportionately born in the state resembling their name, ratio 1.27, and no more likely to stay there, ratio 0.99, p = .45. On marriage he drew a Hispanic subsample of 24,645 couples from the 195,030 Texas licences issued in 2001. The same-initials excess there ran at 1.14 and was carried by couples sharing a whole surname, ratio 1.77; with those excluded the residue was 1.00, chi-square(1) = 0.014, p = .90. Of 95 towns whose founder he could trace, 72% were founded by someone with the matching surname. His companion paper in Psychological Science did the same to the employment finding, on 438,111 American political donors from the 2004 cycle. The overall matching-initial ratio was 2.60, but for people sharing an initial and not the first three letters it was 0.99, and among employers with more than 50 observations 1.01, chi-square(1) = 0.30, p = .583. Sharing three or more letters ran at 64.4, which is what naming a firm after yourself looks like. Pelham and Carvallo replied in the same issue of the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They argue that Simonsohn gives no compelling theoretical reason why implicit egotism should hold only in the laboratory, and that most of his studies have little or no power to reveal real effects. Simonsohn's rejoinder follows on pages 31 to 33. Chatterjee, Mishra and Mishra reported a positive result in the same journal in 2023, and it is evidence of a different kind, described under limits.

study.cite: Simonsohn, U. (2011). Spurious? Name similarity effects (implicit egotism) in marriage, job, and moving decisions. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(1), 1-24.

limits: None of this is experimental, because no one can assign a newborn a name at random and follow it for fifty years. Everything turns on what the base rate should have been, which is what the two sides disagree about. The laboratory finding underneath is not in dispute. Simonsohn calls the evidence of implicit egotism from the laboratory abundant and convincing, and says a modest psychological effect can tip the balance where a chooser is close to indifferent, which is not how a career or a spouse is chosen. Anseel and Duyck gave the field claim its cleanest test. From the Belgian Ministry of Social Security they obtained a third of all full-time private-sector employees, 582,007 records, and counted 36,242 people whose surname initial matched their employer's against 31,952 expected, a ratio of 1.13. Their test across letters was a paired t on 26 values, t(25) = 2.82, p < .01, and they conclude that more than 12,000 Belgians work where they do because the letters matched. Simonsohn gives that sample as 528,007 in his 2011 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology paper and 582,007 in his Psychological Science paper; the original says 582,007. The 2023 result claiming the effect survives controls is not a study of anybody's job. Chatterjee, Mishra and Mishra measured cosine similarity between word vectors for first names and for professions or cities, in word2vec and GloVe models trained on Common Crawl, Twitter, Google News and Google Books. On Common Crawl the mean cosine for matching name and profession was 0.139 against 0.130 for non-matching, p = .0002, with Twitter at 0.154 against 0.142 and Google News at 0.141 against 0.128. Text co-occurrence is not a career, and their own limitations section grants that word representations are weakly linked to world knowledge. Simonsohn names one field study he finds convincing, Chandler, Griffin and Sorensen on donations after hurricanes, ratio 1.24, p = .008; that figure is his description of their paper, which was not obtained here. Two items could not be obtained. Pelham and Carvallo's 2015 paper in Self and Identity reports moderator analyses and is closed at Taylor and Francis, and carries no free copy at Unpaywall, Europe PMC or Semantic Scholar. Sleigh's dental survey is closed at nature.com and at those same three, and was read here at its abstract.
misreadings: Simonsohn is routinely described as having failed to replicate Pelham. He replicated the patterns and attacked the causal reading, and that distinction is the content of his paper. The original career evidence is also far smaller than its fame suggests. In the dentist-versus-lawyer table the female cell that carried the result held 30 women against 21.4 expected. A UK counter-example goes unmentioned in most retellings: Sleigh's survey of the British dental workforce reports that dentists hold dentally related surnames less often than the general population does, calls the gap significant and names it nominative antideterminism, while dental care professionals match the population. The coinage is misattributed. John Hoyland created Feedback and is widely named as the coiner, including by Keaney and colleagues in the BMJ; the column of 17 December 1994 credits the term to a reader, C. R. Cavonius. The founding anecdote is garbled too, and the column garbled it. Splatt and Weedon's 1977 paper treated 40 patients with the Richardson urethroplasty for the urethral syndrome, not incontinence, and 38 improved; the first author is A. J. Splatt, not the J. W. Splatt that New Scientist printed and later writers copied. And the BMJ paper finding that people called Brady need pacemakers is a Christmas issue piece resting on eight Bradys among 579, an odds ratio of 2.27 with a 95% interval of 1.13 to 4.57.
